meta.tagline: Europe's city that never sleeps — being out at 2am here needs no explanation

pills: Eat standing at a tapas bar
Go to El Rastro on Sunday morning

overview.intro: Reset your clock before you land. Lunch starts at 2pm, dinner before 9:30pm is almost unheard of, and at 2am the streets are still full. This isn't an exaggeration — it's Madrid's actual rhythm. See the Prado, visit Reina Sofía, tour the Royal Palace — but if you're already planning what to eat after dinner, you're thinking like a Madrileño. The metro costs less than a café menu. The sun sets late. Tapas are eaten standing, talking, unhurried.

local_word.definition: The ritual of drinking vermouth before lunch. Between noon and 2pm, bars pour vermouth on tap, with crisps, olives, and a slice of tortilla on the side. Sunday after El Rastro, or weekday lunch breaks. 'Shall we do vermuteo?' is one of the most common sentences in a Madrileño's vocabulary.

rules.title: Get into Madrid's rhythm — or the city closes on you
rules.description: Breakfast is light and early. Lunch is between 2pm and 4pm — the most important meal of the day and the cheapest option: a full set menu of starter, main and dessert for 12-15 euros, usually with a drink included. Don't start dinner before 9pm. At 11pm tables are still filling up. Follow these hours and you eat cheaply in local places.

rules.title: Avoid tourist traps — walk two blocks
rules.description: The restaurants around Plaza Mayor, most of Gran Vía and the Mercado de San Miguel are touristy and overpriced. Two blocks away, prices drop and quality rises. If the menu has photos, someone's standing outside inviting you in, or the English menu is very prominent — keep walking.

rules.title: Understand tapas culture
rules.description: In Madrid, tapas don't come free with drinks — some bars put something small out but it's not the rule. Eat standing at the bar, visit a few bars, have something to eat and drink at each one. Small, light, shared: croquetas, patatas bravas, boquerones, a slice of tortilla.

quick_facts.label: Airport
quick_facts.sub: Metro Line 8 to Nuevos Ministerios ~25 min · €3 airport supplement

quick_facts.label: Weather
quick_facts.sub: May–Jun and Sep–Oct ideal · Jul–Aug very hot · Dec–Feb cold

quick_facts.label: Meal times
quick_facts.sub: Menú del día €12–15 · outside these hours places are empty

tip.label: Menú del día — Madrid's best value
tip.text: Monday to Friday, 2–4pm, almost every restaurant has a menú del día. Starter, main and dessert, bread, drink (beer or wine) included — 12 to 15 euros. In tourist areas this is more expensive and generally lower quality. Go down a side street, look for places without an English menu — that's where the real menú del día is.

overview.title: Welcome to Madrid

transport.intro: The metro goes everywhere but the city centre is small enough to walk. Taxis are possible but not necessary.

items.title: Airport → City
items.description: Metro Line 8 to Nuevos Ministerios, 25 minutes, then transfer to the city centre. The ticket is the standard metro fare plus a €3 airport supplement — around €5 total. Fixed-price taxi from the airport: €33. Terminals T1-T2-T3 are connected; T4 is separate, 10 minutes by metro.

items.title: Metro — the city's backbone
items.description: 13 lines, over 300 stations. Single ticket €1.50–2, depending on distance. The 10-trip ticket (MetroBus) is €7.30 — valid on both metro and bus, and can be shared between people (each person taps separately). You need to buy a Multi Card at a station machine first (€2.50). Runs 6am to 1:30am.

items.title: EMT buses — for late nights
items.description: Over 200 daytime routes, 35 night routes (Búho). Daytime runs 6am–11:30pm. Night buses depart from Cibeles — the only option once the metro closes. Pay by card directly or with the 10-trip ticket.

items.title: BiciMAD — electric bikes
items.description: Electric bike sharing stations across the city. €0.50 per 30 minutes or a monthly flat rate of €10. Ideal routes along Paseo del Prado, Retiro and Madrid Río.

items.title: Walking — the best option
items.description: The city centre is smaller than you think. From Sol: La Latina 15 minutes, Malasaña 20 minutes, Chueca 10 minutes. Safe at night. You can spend a full day without needing the metro.

callout.label: Tourist Pass or 10-trip ticket?
callout.text: For a few days, the 10-trip MetroBus ticket (€7.30) is usually better value — valid on both metro and bus, and shareable between travellers. The Tourist Pass is €10 per day for Zone A, €42 for 7 days — unlimited rides including the airport with no supplement. If you're staying more than 3 days and plan to move around a lot, the Tourist Pass is worth considering.

transport.title: Getting Around

stay.intro: Location matters a lot in Madrid — the city lives at night and the neighbourhood's character shapes your evenings directly.

local_word.definition: Neighbourhood. Madrid is made up of dozens of barrios, each with its own identity. The Sol-Gran Vía axis is the tourist centre. La Latina is historic and tapas; Malasaña is young and alternative; Chueca is lively and modern; Chamberí is quiet and local; Lavapiés is multicultural and artistic. Which barrio you stay in determines how you experience the city.

items.name: La Latina / Lavapiés
items.description: La Latina is one of Madrid's oldest neighbourhoods. Cava Baja is lined with tapas bars and historic taverns. Plaza de la Paja is a quiet medieval square. El Rastro passes through on Sundays. Next door, Lavapiés is multicultural, artistic and constantly changing — the Mercado de San Fernando is here.

items.name: Malasaña
items.description: The Movida Madrileña movement of the 1980s was born here. It still carries that spirit: street art, vintage shops, small bars and cafés. Plaza del Dos de Mayo fills up in the evening. Busy but authentic. Ten minutes' walk from Gran Vía but feels like another world.

items.name: Chueca
items.description: Colourful, modern, with a strong nightlife scene. The Mercado de San Antón is here — three floors, with a rooftop bar at the top. Bodega de la Ardosa has been pouring vermouth straight from the barrel since 1892. Shares a border with Malasaña — five minutes between them.

items.name: Chamberí
items.description: The neighbourhood Madrid residents choose when they want to stay in Madrid. Families having morning coffee around Plaza de Olavide, elderly couples sharing newspapers. No tourist pressure. Andén 0 — the ghost metro station — is here. 15-20 minutes' walk to the city centre.

items.name: Barrio de las Letras
items.description: Between the Prado and Puerta del Sol, where Lope de Vega and Cervantes lived. Quotes from writers are set into the pavement of Calle de las Huertas — look down as you walk. The Thyssen and Reina Sofía are within walking distance. It quietens early in the morning — that's when it's at its best.

stay.title: Where to Stay

best_time.intro: Madrid has a continental climate — summers are very hot, winters cold, spring and autumn are excellent.

items.label: Spring
items.name: The best time
items.description: April to June is Madrid's most balanced period. There's sun but the temperature is right for exploring. The rose garden Rosaleda in Retiro Park is in bloom in May. Fiestas de San Isidro in May — Madrid's biggest local festival, street musicians, traditional costumes, open-air concerts. Almond blossom at Quinta de los Molinos in late March.

callout.label: Fiestas de San Isidro — second week of May
callout.text: The festival honouring Madrid's patron saint San Isidro. A full week of open-air concerts across the city, traditional chotis dance performances, local costumes and festivities. The Pradera de San Isidro is the centre — southwest of the city, free. The most authentic local festival.

items.subtitle: Spring · The city opens up, crowds haven't arrived yet

items.label: Autumn
items.name: Breathing after summer
items.description: From mid-September to November Madrid comes back to life. Museums open new exhibitions, restaurants launch new menus. Retiro Park turns golden in autumn — weekday mornings are its finest hours. Crowds are lower than summer.

callout.label: Retiro Park — weekday early morning
callout.text: 350 hectares in the heart of the city. The Palacio de Cristal is a free exhibition space. You can rent a small rowing boat on the lake — go and enjoy it. Weekday mornings at 9am it's a different world from the weekend afternoon crowds. The Fallen Angel statue is on a small hill in the south, with very few visitors.

items.subtitle: Autumn · The city emerges from summer fatigue

items.label: Summer
items.name: Hot but the city never sleeps
items.description: July and August are Madrid's hottest months — 40°C is normal. Between 2pm and 7pm being outside is tough. But nightlife peaks. Veranos de la Villa: open-air concerts, film screenings and cultural events all summer. Picnics by the lake in Casa de Campo. Rooftop bars are at their liveliest this season.

callout.label: Azoteas — Madrid's rooftop bars
callout.text: The Círculo de Bellas Artes rooftop (€5 entry) gives a Gran Vía panorama. The Mercado de San Antón's rooftop bar looks over Chueca. The best spots for sunset views over the city skyline and Gran Vía. Reservations essential in summer.

items.subtitle: Summer · 40°C is possible but nightlife peaks

items.label: Winter
items.name: Quiet but easy on the wallet
items.description: December: Navidad lights cover Gran Vía, and the Reyes Magos parade on the evening of 5 January. January and February are quiet — museums empty, restaurants without queues, hotels affordable. Cocido madrileño — the chickpea winter stew — is the dish of these months. Cold but snow is rare.

callout.label: Reyes Magos — evening of 5 January
callout.text: In Spain it's not Christmas but the Three Kings (Reyes Magos) tradition that matters most. On the evening of 5 January a huge parade through Madrid's streets — three kings and hundreds of floats passing through the city centre, throwing sweets to the crowds. The busiest night of the year. On 6 January morning, children find their gifts.

items.subtitle: Winter · The city quietens, easier on the wallet

monthly_highlights.text: San Isidro: the patron saint's week — picnics on the meadow, chulapo outfits, concerts and the chotis dance.
Terrace season: hot middays drag, but at night the whole city is outdoors; children still on the squares at midnight.
The ideal season: deep blue skies, the heat broken, the culture calendar full — Madrid's sweetest months.
New Year at Puerta del Sol: the ritual of eating 12 grapes with the bells — one grape per chime, and a lucky year if you keep up.

best_time.title: When to Go

eat.intro: Madrid is far from the sea but seafood is among the city's best. And everything here is eaten standing, at the bar, unhurried.

local_word.definition: A bread roll filled with fried calamari. Madrid's street food. Found at bars around Plaza Mayor, especially Bar La Campana. In a city with no coastline, fresh seafood arrives daily thanks to MercaMadrid, one of the world's largest fish markets. This sandwich is the essence of Madrid: simple, delicious, eaten standing up.

items.name: Bocadillo de calamares
items.description: Fried calamari in a bread roll, a squeeze of lemon — that's it. Bar La Campana is right behind Plaza Mayor, open since 1979. There's a queue but it moves fast. A beer alongside, eaten standing in Plaza Mayor. Eat this before you think about where else to go in Madrid.
items.tag: Bar La Campana, behind Plaza Mayor · eat standing · every day

items.name: Huevos rotos
items.description: Fried eggs over crispy potatoes, with jamón or chorizo. The egg is broken so the yolk spreads over the potatoes — that's where the name comes from. Specific to Madrid. Casa Lucio is famous but crowded; you'll find the same dish at smaller bars in La Latina.
items.tag: La Latina bars · lunch and dinner · best shared

items.name: Cocido madrileño
items.description: A stew of chickpeas, pork, chicken, morcilla and vegetables — served in three stages. First the chickpea broth, then the vegetables, then the meats. A winter dish, November to March. Taberna La Bola has been making it since 1870. Advance reservation essential.
items.tag: Winter · lunch · Taberna La Bola since 1870 · reservation required

items.name: Patatas bravas
items.description: Crispy potatoes with two sauces — one spicy (brava), one garlicky aioli. In the Madrid version, the sauce is poured over the potatoes. Every tapas bar has its own recipe. Docamar on Alcalá is the city's most famous patatas bravas bar.
items.tag: Every tapas bar · Docamar is the most famous

items.name: Churros con chocolate
items.description: At the end of a night out at 2am, or Sunday morning with bleary eyes. Chocolatería San Ginés has been open since 1894, right next to Puerta del Sol. Churros straight from the hot oil, chocolate thick and dark. Sitting here late at night is part of the Madrid experience.
items.tag: Chocolatería San Ginés · since 1894 · next to Puerta del Sol · open until 2am

items.name: Vermut ritual
items.description: Sunday after El Rastro or weekday lunch breaks. Vermouth on tap, olives alongside. Bodega de la Ardosa in Chueca has been serving vermouth straight from the barrel since 1892. Casa Alberto in Barrio de las Letras since 1827. This isn't just a drink — it's a ritual of pausing.
items.tag: Sundays after El Rastro or weekday lunch · Bodega de la Ardosa or Casa Alberto

callout.label: How to eat at a tapas bar
callout.text: Go in, find a spot at the bar, say what you want. Eating standing is better than at a table. Visit a few bars: croquetas at one, patatas bravas at the next, bocadillo after that. This is the right way to do tapas in Madrid. Wait a while before asking for the bill — there's no rush here.

eat.title: What to Eat

hidden_gems.intro: Madrid is a big city but its best corners appear as soon as you walk two blocks and turn.

items.name: Andén 0 — Ghost Station
items.description: Under Puerta del Sol metro station, an unused station dating from 1919. Converted into a museum in 2021. Original infrastructure from the construction of the metro preserved — old signs and vehicles. Ticketed; tours at specific times. The starting point of Spain's first metro line.
items.rarity: There's another metro hidden under the metro

items.name: Calle de las Huertas
items.description: In Barrio de las Letras, between Puerta del Sol and the Prado. Quotes from Cervantes, Lope de Vega and other Golden Age writers are set into the pavement of the street where they lived — look down as you walk. Before 10am, before tour groups arrive, there's no crowd. Lope de Vega's house is open as a museum.
items.rarity: Poetry set into the pavement — the literary quarter

items.name: Cerro del Tío Pío — Siete Tetas
items.description: In the Vallecas neighbourhood, walking distance from Line 1 Buenos Aires stop. Seven small hills — known locally as 'Siete Tetas'. One of the least crowded spots in the city for Madrid's skyline and sunset. Bring a picnic blanket and food; sit with the local crowd in the late afternoon.
items.rarity: The city's most local hill for sunset

items.name: Casa Alberto
items.description: In Barrio de las Letras, Calle de las Huertas 18. Open since 1827. Wooden bar, vermouth from the barrel, old Madrid photographs on the walls. Drink the vermouth on tap, order caracoles (snails) alongside — in season.
items.rarity: Open since 1827 — on the same spot

items.name: Quinta de los Molinos
items.description: On Alcalá, near the Ventas bullring. 1,500 almond trees — in late March they all blossom at once, ground and air turning white. Less known than Japanese cherry blossom but equally striking. Free, park always open. Go on a Sunday morning — neighbours walk here.
items.rarity: Almond blossom in March — Madrid's most invisible festival

items.name: Círculo de Bellas Artes Rooftop
items.description: Alcalá 42, right at the corner of Gran Vía. Pay €5 and go up to the rooftop — Gran Vía, the Royal Palace, the Sierra de Guadarrama mountains visible 360 degrees. There's a bar. Inside there are art exhibitions too, often free. Most beautiful at sunset.
items.rarity: Look out over the city from above Gran Vía

callout.label: El Rastro — the Sunday morning ritual
callout.text: Every Sunday 9am–3pm in La Latina. Calle de la Ribera de Curtidores is the main street — second-hand goods, antiques, clothing, books, everything. El Rastro on Sunday, then vermuteo at lunch in La Latina — the standard Madrileño Sunday plan. Watch your pockets, it gets crowded. Best selection in the early morning hours.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Gems

items.label: Eat a bocadillo de calamares
items.sub: Bar La Campana, behind Plaza Mayor. Queue moves fast. Beer alongside, standing in the square.

items.label: Have a menú del día — in the right place
items.sub: Mon–Fri, 2–4pm. Go down a side street, €12–15, full set menu, drink included.

items.label: Go to El Rastro on Sunday morning
items.sub: Before 9am. La Latina, Calle de la Ribera de Curtidores. Vermuteo in the neighbourhood after.

items.label: Walk in Retiro Park on a weekday morning
items.sub: Weekday at 9am. Palacio de Cristal, rose garden, lake. Avoid Sunday afternoons.

items.label: Look down on Calle de las Huertas
items.sub: Barrio de las Letras. Writer quotes set into the pavement. Early morning, before tour groups arrive.

items.label: Churros con chocolate — late night or Sunday morning
items.sub: Chocolatería San Ginés, since 1894. Right next to Puerta del Sol. Open until 2am.

items.label: Go up to the Círculo de Bellas Artes rooftop
items.sub: Alcalá 42, Gran Vía corner. Entry €5. Gran Vía, Royal Palace, mountains. At sunset.

items.label: Do a vermuteo
items.sub: Bodega de la Ardosa (Chueca, 1892) or Casa Alberto (Letras, 1827). Sundays after El Rastro or weekday lunch.

items.label: Do a tapas bar crawl
items.sub: La Latina's Cava Baja or Malasaña. Eat standing, visit a few bars.

items.label: Visit Andén 0
items.sub: Ghost station under Puerta del Sol metro. Dating from 1919. Ticketed, tours at set times.

items.label: Climb Cerro del Tío Pío at sunset
items.sub: Vallecas, Line 1 Buenos Aires. Picnic blanket, food. Madrid skyline, local crowd.

items.label: Visit the Prado or Reina Sofía
items.sub: Prado free Tue–Sat 6–8pm. Reina Sofía free Mon–Sat 7–9pm, Sun 1:30–7pm.

checklist.title: Madrid Checklist
checklist.completion_message: You've lived Madrid at its own pace. Next time, stay out even later.

traps.title: Skip the Traps
traps.intro: Madrid is a generous city; its traps are squeezed into its three most touristic squares. Know these four — the rest is safe ground.

items.name: Sitting down on Plaza Mayor
items.description: The square's terraces sell the historic view, not the kitchen: frozen calamares, double-priced sangria.
items.instead: Walk the square, take your photo; eat your bocadillo de calamares standing at the classic bars just outside it.

items.name: Mistaking Mercado San Miguel for a 'real market'
items.description: The glass market is beautiful, but it's now a tourist showcase: small portions, big bills.
items.instead: For the real market experience go to Mercado de la Cebada or Antón Martín; same flavours, half the price, full of locals.

items.name: Shell games and petitions at Sol
items.description: The cup game, the 'deaf association petition' and the rosemary-sprig fortune tellers around Puerta del Sol are the same crew in different costumes.
items.instead: Don't stop, smile, walk on; bag in front, phone in pocket. Even watching serves the crew's crowd trick.

items.name: Bus-tour flamenco 'galas'
items.description: The giant dinner-hall shows don't carry flamenco's soul; Madrid's tablao tradition is smaller and truer.
items.instead: Pick an established tablao, eat elsewhere, watch the show with a drink: cheaper and many times more moving.

callout.label: The golden rule
callout.text: Madrid's rule is simple: walk two blocks from any tourist square and the price halves while the flavour doubles. The city is already telling you this; listen.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Routes
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. The times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: Art, a park and midnight churros

steps.title: The Prado — first hour
steps.description: Book ahead and meet Velázquez and Goya with a fresh head; two hours is enough — don't attempt it all.

steps.title: Retiro Park
steps.description: The Crystal Palace, a rowboat on the pond, or simply sun on a bench: where Madrid breathes.

steps.title: Long lunch in La Latina
steps.description: Bar to bar along Cava Baja: huevos rotos, tortilla, a glass of vermut. Hurrying is forbidden.

steps.title: Malasaña + Chueca crawl
steps.description: Vintage shops, record stores, third-wave coffee; Madrid's young heart beats in these two quarters.

steps.title: Sunset on the Círculo rooftop
steps.description: Look down Gran Vía from the Círculo de Bellas Artes terrace: the city's lights switch on at exactly this hour.

steps.title: Churros at San Ginés
steps.description: Dipping churros in thick hot chocolate at midnight is Madrid's closing ritual; the queue moves fast.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Live the city as a guest, not a tourist

steps.title: The classics
steps.description: The 1-day flow above: Prado, Retiro, La Latina, the rooftop.

steps.title: The palace and hidden Madrid
steps.description: The Royal Palace and Almudena in the morning, the Andén 0 ghost station in Chamberí at noon, tapas in Barrio de las Letras + Casa Alberto at night.

steps.title: Market and goodbye
steps.description: El Rastro flea market if it's Sunday, then vermut hour in La Latina; Guernica at the Reina Sofía in the afternoon, farewell with the skyline from Cerro del Tío Pío at dusk.

phrases.title: The 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: Madrid is patient with English, but five Spanish words open the doors wide.

items.meaning: The short all-day greeting — entering any bar or shop
Please — add it to the end of your order
Cheers! — vermut glasses rise to this
OK / deal — Spain's most used word; said twice: vale, vale
